title: What is an Atom?
summary: Protons, neutrons, electrons and the nucleus.
content:
Everything around you is made of atoms. An atom has a tiny, dense nucleus containing positively charged protons and neutral neutrons. Negatively charged electrons move around the nucleus in shells.

  • Atomic number (Z) = number of protons
  • Mass number (A) = protons + neutrons
  • A neutral atom has equal protons and electrons

Example: Carbon-12 has 6 protons, 6 neutrons and 6 electrons.

title: Reading the Periodic Table
content:
The periodic table arranges elements by increasing atomic number. Vertical columns are groups (1–18) and horizontal rows are periods (1–7).

  • Group 1: alkali metals — very reactive
  • Group 17: halogens — reactive non-metals
  • Group 18: noble gases — very unreactive

Elements in the same group have the same number of valence electrons, so they behave similarly.

title: Electron Configuration
summary: How electrons fill shells and subshells.
content:
Electrons fill orbitals in order of increasing energy (the Aufbau principle): 1s, 2s, 2p, 3s, 3p, 4s, 3d, 4p …

Each s subshell holds 2 electrons, p holds 6, d holds 10 and f holds 14.

Example: Sodium (Z = 11) → 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s¹. The single 3s electron makes sodium very reactive.

title: Chemical Bonding
content:
Atoms bond to reach a stable electron arrangement.

  • Ionic bond: electrons are transferred (e.g. Na⁺Cl⁻)
  • Covalent bond: electrons are shared (e.g. H–H, O=O)
  • Metallic bond: a sea of delocalised electrons around metal ions

Try drawing H2O and CO2 in the Structure Drawer to see single and double bonds.

title: The Mole Concept
content:
One mole contains 6.022 × 10²³ particles (Avogadro's number).

Molar mass is the mass of one mole in grams: add up atomic masses. H2O = 2 × 1.008 + 15.999 = 18.015 g/mol.

moles = mass ÷ molar mass. Use the Molar Mass Calculator to practise.

title: Balancing Equations
summary: Law of conservation of mass in action.
content:
Atoms are neither created nor destroyed in a reaction, so both sides must contain the same number of each atom.

Unbalanced: H2 + O2 → H2O
Balanced: 2H2 + O2 → 2H2O

Only change coefficients, never subscripts. Check your answers with the Equation Balancer.

title: Melting & Boiling Points
summary: Why substances melt and boil at different temperatures.
content:
The melting point is where a solid becomes liquid; the boiling point is where a liquid becomes gas.

Stronger forces between particles mean higher melting and boiling points. Ionic NaCl melts at 801 °C, while methane (weak forces) boils at −161.5 °C.

Hydrogen bonding gives water an unusually high boiling point for its size.

title: Acids and Bases
content:
Acids release H⁺ ions in water; bases release OH⁻ ions.

  • pH < 7: acidic
  • pH = 7: neutral
  • pH > 7: basic

Neutralisation: HCl + NaOH → NaCl + H2O.

title: Types of Chemical Reactions
content:
Most reactions you meet at school fit a few patterns:

  • Synthesis: A + B → AB (2H2 + O2 → 2H2O)
  • Decomposition: AB → A + B (CaCO3 → CaO + CO2)
  • Single displacement: A + BC → AC + B (Zn + 2HCl → ZnCl2 + H2)
  • Double displacement: AB + CD → AD + CB (AgNO3 + NaCl → AgCl + NaNO3)
  • Combustion: fuel + O2 → CO2 + H2O

Try building each one in the Reaction Builder.

title: Organic Chemistry Basics
content:
Organic chemistry is the chemistry of carbon compounds. Carbon forms four bonds and can make chains and rings.

  • Alkanes (single bonds): methane CH4, ethane C2H6
  • Alkenes (C=C): ethene C2H4
  • Alkynes (C≡C): ethyne C2H2

A functional group decides how a molecule reacts: –OH (alcohols), –COOH (carboxylic acids), C=O (aldehydes and ketones), –NH2 (amines).

Draw ethanol in the Structure Lab and find its –OH group.

title: The Gas Laws
summary: Boyle, Charles and the ideal gas equation.
content:
Gases are described by pressure (P), volume (V), temperature (T, in kelvin) and amount (n).

  • Boyle's law: at constant T, PV = constant
  • Charles's law: at constant P, V/T = constant
  • Ideal gas law: PV = nRT, with R = 0.08206 L·atm·mol⁻¹·K⁻¹

Explore these in the Gas Laws experiment of the Lab Simulator.

title: Laboratory Safety
summary: Rules that keep every chemist safe.
content:
• Always wear safety goggles and a lab coat.
  • Never taste chemicals or smell them directly – waft vapours towards you.
  • Add acid to water, never water to acid.
  • Know where the eyewash, shower and fire extinguisher are.
  • Read hazard symbols and the Safety Data Sheet before using a chemical.
  • Dispose of chemicals as your teacher instructs.

CHEMVERSE experiments are virtual – do not repeat them at home.
